title: Texts, audience and purpose
summary: What counts as a text, who it is for and what it is trying to do: the starting point for every analysis in this course.

keyterms.definition: Any crafted piece of communication that can be analysed, from a novel or poem to an advert, tweet, photograph or speech.
The readers, viewers or listeners a text is aimed at; the intended audience shapes vocabulary, tone, content and form.
What a text aims to achieve, such as to persuade, inform, entertain, provoke, commemorate or sell.
The level of formality in language, chosen to suit the audience, purpose and situation.
The attitude a text conveys towards its subject or audience, e.g. urgent, ironic, warm or detached.
How a text speaks to its audience, e.g. directly with 'you', inclusively with 'we', or impersonally.
A text valued for its artistic use of language and form, such as a poem, novel, short story or play.
A text mainly designed for a practical, social or commercial function, such as an advert, article, speech or infographic.
The kind of reader a text seems to assume, revealed by what it explains, takes for granted or values.
A specific group a text is designed to reach, often defined by age, interests, values or needs.

lessons.title: Who is it for and why?

questions.prompt: A leaflet says: "Got a spare hour on Saturdays? Help us turn the old car park into a garden everyone can enjoy." What is its main purpose?
options: To inform readers about the history of the car park
To persuade local residents to volunteer
To entertain readers with a story
To criticise the council for neglect
questions.explanation: The direct question and the invitation to 'help us' show a persuasive purpose aimed at recruiting volunteers.

questions.statement: In this course, a photograph, a cereal box and a tweet can all be treated as texts.
questions.explanation: Language and literature uses a broad definition of 'text': any crafted communication whose choices can be analysed.

questions.text: The level of formality a writer chooses, such as formal or colloquial, is called ___.
questions.explanation: Register describes formality. Tone is the attitude expressed; the two often work together.

questions.prompt: "Yo! Grab your mates and smash the summer with our NEW fizz!" Which audience is most likely targeted?
questions.explanation: Slang ('Yo', 'mates', 'smash'), exclamations and a focus on socialising suggest a young target audience.

questions.prompt: Match each text to its most likely main purpose.
questions.explanation: Most texts have a primary purpose, though many combine several (an advert may entertain in order to persuade).

questions.prompt: A sentence reads: "We all know that feeling when the alarm goes off on a Monday." What mode of address is used?
questions.explanation: 'We all know' creates an inclusive mode of address, building shared experience and rapport with the reader.

questions.statement: A text can only ever have one purpose.
questions.explanation: Texts often have layered purposes: a public health advert may inform, shock and persuade at the same time.

questions.text: The attitude a text conveys, for example bitter, playful or reverent, is its ___.
questions.explanation: Tone is the attitude or feeling conveyed; analyse which word choices create it.

questions.prompt: Which feature most clearly marks a text as literary rather than non-literary?
options: Its main value lies in its artistic use of language and form
It was written by a famous person
questions.explanation: Literary texts are valued chiefly for their aesthetic, imaginative use of language. The boundary is blurry and itself worth discussing.

questions.prompt: Put these first steps for approaching an unseen text in a sensible order.
items: Work out the audience and purpose
Note key features of language and structure
Explain how those features achieve the purpose
questions.explanation: Moving from what the text is, to whom and why, to how, keeps analysis focused on effect.

questions.prompt: A travel article says: "Skip the tourist traps; you've seen the Eiffel Tower on a thousand postcards." What does this suggest about the implied reader?
options: They see themselves as an experienced, independent traveller
They work in the tourism industry
questions.explanation: The text assumes the reader already knows famous sights and wants something more authentic, flattering a self-image of the savvy traveller.

questions.statement: The implied reader is always the same person as the actual reader.
questions.explanation: The implied reader is constructed by the text. Real readers may resist or fall outside that role, which can produce critical readings.

questions.text: Using the pronoun "you" to speak to the reader directly is called direct ___.
questions.explanation: Direct address involves the reader personally and is common in advertising and speeches.

questions.prompt: A bank's website explains: "An ISA is a tax-free savings account." What does the definition reveal about the target audience?
options: They may be new to saving or investing
questions.explanation: Explaining basic terms implies readers who might not know them, so the text targets newcomers.

questions.prompt: Which register best suits a letter of complaint to an airline?
questions.explanation: A formal, measured register signals seriousness and makes the complaint more likely to be taken seriously.

questions.prompt: Match the mode of address to its example.

pairs.right: Applications must be received by Friday.
Isn't it time you treated yourself?

questions.explanation: Each mode positions the reader differently: commanded, included, kept at a distance or invited to agree.

questions.statement: Shifts in tone within a text are worth analysing because they often mark a change in purpose or argument.
questions.explanation: A move from humour to seriousness, for instance, often signals the key message. Track tone shifts across the structure.

questions.text: A specific group a text is designed to reach, such as new parents or gamers, is its ___ audience.
questions.explanation: Defining the target audience precisely helps explain the writer's choices.

questions.prompt: Why is "the audience is everyone" a weak claim in a Paper 1 answer?
options: Because it does not explain any specific choice the writer has made
Because only literary texts have audiences
questions.explanation: Strong answers define the audience precisely and use that to explain particular choices of language, image and structure.

questions.prompt: A recipe blog opens with a long personal story before the recipe. Which purpose does the story mainly serve?
options: To build a relationship with readers and a personal brand
questions.explanation: Personal anecdote builds trust and a sense of community, keeping readers returning; the blog form rewards personality.
